blocks.text: Mass attached to an elastic spring

Consider a body of mass m attached to a spring of spring constant k on a smooth horizontal surface (Fig 14.2). At first it rests at O, the mean position. A force F displaces it from O to A through a displacement x to the right. By Hooke's law the applied force is proportional to the displacement: F = kx (14.1). The spring exerts an elastic restoring force on the body that is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction: F = -kx (14.2). When the applied force is removed, the body moves back towards O, crosses O because of its inertia, reaches B where the spring is compressed, returns, and so oscillates between A and B.

By Newton's second law F = ma (14.3). Comparing with (14.2), ma = -kx, so a = -(k/m) x (14.4). Since k/m is constant, a = -(constant) x, or a proportional to -x. This is the mathematical form of simple harmonic motion: the acceleration of a body executing S.H.M. is always directly proportional to its displacement and always directed towards the mean position.

Time period and frequency: comparing a = -(k/m)x with a = -w^2 x gives w^2 = k/m, so w = square root of (k/m). Since w = 2 pi f, f = (1/2 pi) square root of (k/m) and T = 1/f = 2 pi square root of (m/k).

blocks.alt: Three rows: a mass m on a spring fixed to a wall. Top: at rest at the mean position O, marked by a dashed vertical line. Middle: pulled to A, a distance x to the right of O; the spring pulls back with F = -kx, shown by a red arrow to the left. Bottom: released, the mass overshoots to B with the spring compressed, and a red arrow to the right shows the spring pushing back. Below: F = -kx and F = ma so a = -(k/m)x = -w^2 x; w = sqrt(k/m), f = (1/2 pi) sqrt(k/m), T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k).
blocks.caption: A mass on a spring executing S.H.M. (original diagram after Fig 14.2).
blocks.long_description: Whichever side the mass is on, the spring force points back towards O, and it is larger the further the mass is from O. That is exactly the condition a = -(constant) x for S.H.M.

blocks.title: Point to ponder
blocks.text: Real-world applications of the S.H.M. principle include pendulum clocks, musical instruments and vehicle suspension systems.

A particle executing S.H.M. has an angular frequency of 2 rad s^-1. Find its frequency and time period. Solution: w = 2 pi f, so f = w / 2 pi = 2 / 2 pi = 1/pi, about 0.318 Hz. T = 1/f = pi, about 3.14 s.

blocks.title: Interesting information
blocks.text: The Dutch mathematician, astronomer and physicist Christiaan Huygens patented the first pendulum clock in 1656. He worked out the mathematical formula relating a pendulum's length to its time period, using simple harmonic motion.

A simple pendulum is a small, heavy bob of mass m hung from a rigid support by a light, inextensible string of length l. When it is displaced from its mean position O to an extreme position P and released, a restoring force acts towards O and the bob oscillates to and fro along a curved path under gravity (Fig 14.3).

At P the string makes an angle theta with the vertical. The weight mg can be resolved into mg cos(theta) along the string and mg sin(theta) perpendicular to it. Since the bob does not move along the string, mg cos(theta) and the tension T cancel. The component mg sin(theta) is the restoring force towards O: F = -mg sin(theta). With F = ma, a = -g sin(theta) (14.5). For small angles, sin(theta) is approximately equal to theta in radians (Table 14.1), so a = -g theta (14.6). Since theta = S/l, where S is the arc length, and for small angles the displacement x is nearly equal to S, a = -(g/l) x (14.7). With l and g constant, a is proportional to -x: the motion of a simple pendulum is S.H.M.

blocks.caption: Table 14.1 Values of theta and sin(theta) for small angles

blocks.text: Comparing a = -(g/l)x with a = -w^2 x (14.8): w^2 = g/l, so w = square root of (g/l) (14.9). Since w = 2 pi f, f = (1/2 pi) square root of (g/l) and T = 1/f = 2 pi square root of (l/g) (14.10). So the period of a simple pendulum is directly proportional to the square root of its length and inversely proportional to the square root of g; it does not depend on the mass of the bob or (for small swings) on the amplitude. A pendulum whose period is two seconds is called a second pendulum.

blocks.alt: Left: a pendulum of length l displaced through angle theta from the vertical dashed line through O. At the bob, the tension T acts up the string, the weight mg acts straight down, and mg is split into mg cos(theta) along the string and mg sin(theta) at right angles to it, pointing back towards O. Right: the steps F = -mg sin(theta), so a = -g sin(theta); for small angles sin(theta) = theta = x/l; a = -(g/l)x = -w^2 x; w = sqrt(g/l); T = 2 pi sqrt(l/g); g = 4 pi^2 l / T^2.
blocks.caption: Forces on a simple pendulum (original diagram after Fig 14.3).
blocks.long_description: Only the part of the weight across the string, mg sin(theta), pulls the bob back. For small angles this is proportional to the displacement, so the pendulum moves in S.H.M.

blocks.text: Using a simple pendulum to measure g
Measure the length l of the pendulum, set it swinging with a small amplitude and time it with a stopwatch to find T. Then g = 4 pi^2 l / T^2.

What is the length of a second pendulum where g = 9.8 m s^-2? Solution: T = 2 s and T = 2 pi square root of (l/g), so T^2 = 4 pi^2 l / g and l = g T^2 / (4 pi^2) = (9.8 m s^-2)(2 s)^2 / (4 x 3.14^2) = 0.994 m, or 99.4 cm. Its frequency is f = 1/T = 0.5 Hz.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: The word pendulum comes from the Latin word pendulus, meaning hanging.
